utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom, and good morning to you, Ms. Lindsay, again. Unexpectedly, I see you on your feet, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I would like just a brief preliminary this morning. I would like to move to withdraw my previous request to bring back General Obradovic. And the reason for that would be that the main point I was trying to get to with General Obradovic was to take him to the area of the military police and security regarding prisoners of war, their responsibilities and duties, both in the regulations and in the practice. This is where I was going, because that was specifically left out in a cross-examination or avoided. Yesterday, you'll recall Mr. Thayer went over some of those regulations regarding the military police and the security, and their responsibilities in relation to prisoners of war; of course, a central issue to the case. When those rules and regulations were gone over and explained, and I think bringing the general back to re-explain that would be repetitive and, in this context, not essential. So in weighing everything, I thought that it is not essential to bring him back and ask him those very things that just came in, I thought, clearly. The other issues that I had mentioned related to some of the other issues. I think those will be dealt with with other witnesses. So I would ask your leave to withdraw the request from bringing General Obradovic back for the reasons stated. And I've had a chance to explain this also to Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't see a need that the Defence wants to respond. The Chamber will consider that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence is satisfied to hear that the Prosecution decided not to recall the Witness Obradovic. The Defence is of the view that it is not necessary to recall him. I would also like to remind everybody that the witness should be notified in an appropriate way that he does not have the duty anymore to observe all those things that he was warned about at the beginning of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Indeed, the Chamber will grant leave not to recall the witness. The witness, and I would like to put it on the record, is released from his duties as a witness in this trial, and he should be notified accordingly. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Welcome, Mr. Thayer. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a request to make on behalf of Mr. Nikolic. Virginia Lindsay, on behalf of Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: Good morning. He was shown a document this morning that he hasn't seen in quite a while, and he has requested that he be supplied a copy of it so that he can use it to refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to invite the witness to sit down. Please sit down. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To which document are you referring?

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: It would be Defence D00203. The title of the document is "Rules of Service, Security Organs for the SFRY."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees this document should be forwarded to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On your request, you have now received this document you asked for to have the opportunity to look through it. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before Mr. Thayer is continuing his examination-in-chief, I would ask you for a clarification to a topic we discussed yesterday. We saw a document signed by Lieutenant-Colonel - I'm not sure if I recall the name correctly - Ognjenovic. I don't recall. But he was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. You qualified his position as a politician, and I asked you about that yesterday. I would like to ask you for some more detailed clarification. Did this man ever have a political post in a political party or the post in the state organisation, apart from his posts in the army? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know is that Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic only had a function in the military. So as far as I know, he was never in the political parties there. And I also think that while he was in Bratunac, he was also not in any of the political parties. But I want to clarify one thing. Maybe it was I who caused the confusion. Mr. President, there are political functions in the military, so within the army, there are political functions. While I was in the army, we used to call them political commissars. The information that I have is that Mr. Ognjenovic, while he served in the army, having graduated from the Military Academy, performed various political functions of this kind within the army. In the army, you have assistant commanders for moral and political work and then assistant commanders for moral and political training. So when I was speaking about him, I meant that kind of political functions. And another thing that I forgot to tell you yesterday: The first time that Mr. Ognjenovic arrived to my brigade, and I told you already he was within the brigade twice on two different occasions, he arrived in a blue uniform. Now, as far as I know, that means that he came from a specific combat branch, and that is air forces and the air defence. So the essence of what I wanted to say was that Mr. Ognjenovic was not an infantryman, that he was not a commander, that he had never commanded such a big establishment as a brigade. That's what I know. Now, what other functions he performed earlier, I don't know, especially not chronologically speaking. I never knew him before he arrived at Bratunac. But what I heard from others is that some time before the conflict, he had been employed in Rajlovac, in the Military High School. He was a teacher in that Military High School. That's what I know. So, in conclusion, why did I say that he was a politician? I said it because I knew at the time, and I also know now, that within the military he used to perform functions of a political character. He was assistant for political issues to the commanders who actually commanded units. That's what I meant when I said that he was a politician. I did not mean to say that he was a member of a political party. While I was in the military and while Ognjenovic was in the military, the military was de-politicised. Members of the military could not be members of political parties, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. Mr. Thayer, please continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning to the Defence. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And good morning again, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have P2158 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while that's coming up: Sir, do you remember the years during which Colonel Ognjenovic served as the commander of the Bratunac Brigade? You indicated that he served two tours or two terms of duty in the Bratunac Brigade. Can you recall which years those were? Obviously, we have here a document from July of 1994, at which time he was commander. Do you remember what year his other tour as commander was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about his first tour of duty. Now we are talking about the period when Mr. Ognjenovic was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. I think that before that, Commander Ognjenovic performed the duty of the Chief of Staff, but I am not sure. I wouldn't like to speculate now. I don't know exactly when he was appointed to the Bratunac Brigade, but I know that he was there twice, first as the Chief of Staff and the second time as the brigade commander. I don't know the dates, and I don't want to speculate about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in terms of the establishment, do you recall whether, when Colonel Ognjenovic served as Chief of Staff of the Bratunac Brigade, whether that meant that he simultaneously held any other position within the brigade when he was Chief of Staff? Does that mean at the same time, he also holds another position within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this other function. I know that in the military, there is the establishment that puts you in a certain position, and if you are a Chief of Staff, then you cannot be anything else within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was -- whether we're talking about Colonel Ognjenovic or Colonel Blagojevic, whichever commander we're speaking about, do you know who would have occupied the position of deputy commander in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I speak about the establishment, regardless of the brigade, itself, as far as I remember the establishment, every brigade has a commander and a Chief of Staff. Functionally speaking, the Chief of Staff is also the deputy commander, as far as I can remember. However, I'm not absolutely sure about it. I don't know enough about the establishment. If I knew the establishment in its entirety, then I could speak about it authoritatively. But what I do know is in the absence of the commander, the Chief of Staff stands in for the commander. Now, whether the establishment stipulates that at the same time, he has the function of the deputy commander, that I don't know. For that, we would have to look into the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, given the length of time you served in the Bratunac Brigade from late 1992 through the end of the war, can you give the Trial Chamber a sense of the authorities which are invested or carried by the commander of the brigade? You've spoken about your duties and responsibilities, what you were permitted to do, your relationships with various units and other officers, but can you give the Trial Chamber some idea of, really, what the role of the commander, as you experienced it in the Bratunac Brigade, was? And if you need to compare one with the other, if you think that's helpful, that's fine. If not, that's okay too. But please give the Trial Chamber some sense of what the actual role of the commander was, the responsibilities, authorities and rights that that commander had within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a rather complex issue. I can only speak on the basis of my personal experience and for myself. I never had anything to do with command and control. I emphasise again that I can speak, in principle, based on my experience about what a commander does, but only about my brigade. Whether the situation was the same in all the brigades, I wouldn't know. I can only tell you with some precision what my commander used to do. So the brigade commander is an authorised official. He performs direct command and control over the units within the brigade. This command and control is accomplished through the commanders of subordinate units. So in my brigade, the brigade commander was the person who commanded the battalions and all other units that comprised my brigade. I'm talking here about the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. Moreover, the battalion commander carries out all his tasks through consultations and with the help of his assistants. Those assistants usually have their functions within certain areas of responsibility. The commander plans, organises and commands with the help of his assistants. The assistants in my brigade were the assistant commander for logistics - if you need the name, I can give you the names of all the assistants. Then assistant commander for organisation, manning and personnel. Then assistant commander for moral, religious and legal affairs. Then assistant commander -- or, rather, chief for intelligence/security affairs within the brigade. And assistant commander for operations and training. So they are assistant commanders or chiefs of organs that comprise the inner core of the command. This inner core of the command, together with the commander, plans, makes decisions, proposes anything related about the use and command of units. During the command and control over the units, as far as I know about how it used to be in my brigade, the brigade commander is at the top. I already explained yesterday, regardless of the proposals that he receives from his subordinate officers in the brigade command, it is the brigade commander who has the exclusive right to make decisions about the use of units that belong to the brigade that he commands. Also, the brigade commander is the person who initiates disciplinary proceedings against all those who are in breach of military order and discipline. That's how it functioned where I was. The commander was the person who would sign criminal reports prepared by the organ that he authorised to perform these duties. In my brigade, there was a person authorised to prepare such criminal reports. So to put it in one sentence: The brigade commander is the officer who plans, organises, commands, co-ordinates and controls the units from within the brigade or, in other words, the brigade. This is in the briefest terms. If you have any further specific questions about the practice as it was in my brigade, I am going to try to explain that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your brigade, sir, what was the practice when the brigade commander issued an order? What was the practice that was followed by the subordinate members of your brigade when the commander issued an order to them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my brigade, this went as follows: After an order would be issued, an order of any kind -- and of course I have to say that before an order was issued, usually there were meetings, consultations and other things. But when an order is issued by the brigade commander, the subordinates - and here I'm referring, first of all, to the battalion commanders - have the duty to carry out the order exactly as it was ordered by the commander. Furthermore, the subordinates must, while carrying out the order, inform the commander if there were any problems in carrying out that order. Of course, if there are no problems, then after the task had been carried out, the subordinates have to report back to the commander that the order had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday, sir, in connection with this report from Commander Ognjenovic that went out to all the battalions, and then to the units even below the battalions, and you told us yesterday that one of the results of this report was a lack of discipline among some of the soldiers. And we're going to talk about, in a little while, some of the sniping that happened that you've testified about before, but what I want to focus on right now, sir, is: When you spoke about this order, resulting in a lack of discipline, can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit how, in your experience in your brigade, serving under different commanders, how the personality of the commander, through his conduct or through his orders, was communicated to you and whether it had any effect on the subordinate members of the brigade? And that's a long question. I'm going to wait a minute, and then I'm going to try to simplify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, I would appreciate if you could put the questions in a shorter manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question again, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber a sense of how the commanders under whom you served, be it Colonel Ognjenovic, be it Colonel Blagojevic, how their personalities were reflected in their command style? I'll start there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your first question, although it was a lengthy one. However, the second one is more specific. My answer is that the entire atmosphere in the brigade, in the unit -- or, rather, in any unit, in my view, depends on the authority of the officer who commands that unit. As for anything else -- I'm saying all of this to you on the basis of my own experience because I lived through all this. Everything else depends on his attitude vis-a-vis certain questions or certain problems or activities. In my case, in my brigade, I certainly do not want to compare Colonel Blagojevic and Colonel Ognjenovic. Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic, in the relevant period of time that we are discussing, as I have said previously, created a true alibi through this information for the lack of discipline that was later manifested along the separation lines facing the enclave. May I support this by saying to you that there were certain things that were actually happening on the ground that were facts. Regardless of all obligations vis-a-vis the protected area of Srebrenica, after this information certain combat activities were carried out by the Bratunac Brigade in the following sense: The border of the enclave was crossed, and the unit entered the area that was under the control of the UN, or, rather, the Dutch Battalion. What I claim with certainty now is that in this period, there was an entry in Perska Kosa, Trig 413. Also, there was another violation of the enclave on the positions of the 1st Infantry Battalion. And what I know and what I recorded was a violation of the separation line within the area of Pribicevac, in the area of the 3rd Battalion. In addition to that, in addition to these incursions, this lack of discipline, these combat activities that were not appropriate in that situation, and they could not really yield any effect, as far as the Bratunac Brigade was concerned, quite simply they, themselves, impaired the relationship that we had with the Dutch Battalion and even the minimum confidence that was there was destroyed between the Serb side and the forces that were in the protected zone; that is to say, UNPROFOR. I was liaison officer - I said that yesterday - and I could not explain in any way why the Serb forces, the members of my own brigade, were entering the safe area and threatening its security. I'm going to be quite frank here. I tried to think of all sorts of explanations; that the Muslims were jeopardising our positions, that we were under threat. These were the pretexts, excuses that I used, because I really had nothing to say to the people from the Dutch Battalion, because they are professionals who record and locate exactly the time of these incursions and everything else. I tried to justify that because I was accused [as interpreted] to do so by Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic. He insisted that every time when I went to these meetings to resolve the problems that had cropped up, that I say over there, quite simply, the Muslim forces were threatening the positions of the Serb forces, that they wanted to enter our territory, that they were ambushing our troops. Of course, there were such intentions during this period of time as well. However, in these three specific cases that I'm speaking about, that was not the intention involved. And there were no activities in Perska Kosa, the 1st Infantry Battalion or in the area of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, and that is this lack of discipline. It had assumed the nature of organised incursions, combat activities, and threats to the safe area of Srebrenica. In addition to that, what I mentioned yesterday were the so-called sniper activities, sniping that was there from the Serb side but also from the Muslim side, from the enclave. Quite simply, throughout this confusion, there was this lack of confidence that was created. I, as liaison officer, had a great deal of problems in that respect to explain what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To understand the situation a little bit better, I would like to ask you: When did the term of service as a brigade commander of Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic end? Was it terminated at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, sometime -- well, what I remember the best is just before the planning of the Srebrenica operation, so I'm not sure. I don't know the date on which he was relieved of duty, but I know that he was succeeded by Colonel Blagojevic. It could be even 1995, but I really do not know the dates; I never really dwelled on that. I never saw their personnel records, I never saw the documents related to their appointments, the termination of their duties, et cetera. At any rate, it was 1995, before the planning of the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I think we have some documents that are historical documents that can establish that pretty easily, and I don't think we'll have any objection from the Defence. And we can either offer it from the Bar or get it in through another witness, but we can deal with that, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We received an answer -- I received an answer I was asking for. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down in the English, please. And if we could go to the second page in English, please, sorry. And we'll need to go to the second page in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, at the top of the -- towards the top of the page in the original, Colonel Ognjenovic writes: "We have won the war in Podrinje." Can you just tell us what that word -- that name "Podrinje" refers to? When we speak of -- or when one speaks of the Podrinje, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When speaking of Podrinje, what is meant is part of the municipality or part of the territory that is along the Drina River. In my state where I live, that area is called "Podrinje," conditionally speaking. It is Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica, Visegrad, Foca, those municipalities. Perhaps I went a bit too far, but, anyway, that is the area that is along the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We're done with this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've spoken a couple of times about sniping. Let's have a look at some documents. May we have 65 ter 5906, please. I beg your pardon. Before we do that, I want to look at one other document. May we have 65 ter 1908, please. Let me know when you've had a chance to look at this first page, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We have here an order. We can see the date is the 24th of July, about 20 days after Colonel Ognjenovic's report was issued, which we just saw. This is coming from the Command of the Drina Corps. The heading is: "Defining tasks from the briefing and urging their completion," and an order follows. And we can see -- and we'll see, you know, in a couple of minutes, the signature page is General Zivanovic signing this order. We can see here that General Zivanovic writes that: "Pursuant to a briefing on 1 July 1994 to the VRS Main Staff commander by the Drina Corps commander and regiment-brigade commanders about the level of combat readiness in units and corps commands ..." He issues the following order. And in this portion, he refers to a prior Main Staff order, and he gives the number, and it's dated the 22nd of July, 1994. Do you see that section, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this reference to a briefing concerning the level of combat readiness in the units, can you tell the Trial Chamber what that refers to, this combat readiness briefing?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that in the Army of Republika Srpska, and I hope that that is the case in other armies as well, but, anyway, I will be speaking about the Army of Republika Srpska, there is this so-called briefing about the state of combat readiness in units. In this specific case, it has to do with a briefing with the commander of the Main Staff. And I think that this is the semi-annual report on the state of combat readiness, the 1st of July, 1994, so the state of combat readiness is assessed twice a year, as far as I know. Perhaps it's done more frequently, but I know the practice that prevailed in my unit. Combat readiness or the analysis of combat readiness is the analysis of the overall state of combat readiness, in terms of all its elements. And the elements of combat readiness are precisely those elements that I spoke of previously. Namely, command and control is analysed, then what is analysed is combat training, then organisation, mobilisation and personnel affairs, then logistics affairs, and intelligence and security activities. When the semi-annual or annual combat report is being written up, then the assistant commanders prepare their own contributions in their respective lines of work. That is to say, every assistant commander and head of organ is duty-bound to prepare a particular part of that semi-annual or annual report on combat readiness in the unit, and we did that regularly. After these contributions are prepared, then there is a briefing to the commander at a meeting. What is presented is everything that had been written up and everything that had been done. Of course, what is presented is the overall situation; namely, the favourable developments that were there and also things that were an obstacle in the path of working better, and proposals as to how work could be improved in the coming period. Of course, once the commander approves of this - that is, the practice of my brigade - then all of that is written up, presented in written form, and then this proposal -- or, rather, this contribution to the analysis on combat readiness is submitted to the commander. He brings all of this together, compiling a single document, and the document is entitled "Analysis of Combat Readiness" for such and such a period. And this kind of report of combat readiness, this kind of analysis, is what the commander ultimately assesses by providing a grade that he believes is appropriate in terms of everything that had happened. This kind of report on combat readiness is submitted to the superior command once the commander had signed it and approved it, and then, of course, at higher levels. I never took part in this, but I do know that at higher levels also -- I mean, I spoke about brigade level. I think that the procedure is absolutely the same at the level of corps command and the level of Main Staff. That is to say, that this is the way it is done at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's spend a couple of minutes and look at this order from General Zivanovic, and then I want to put a couple of questions to you about it. If we can go to the next page in English, and this will -- we can stay on the first page in B/C/S. We just focus on number 3. We can see that General Zivanovic orders that: "No equipment is to be allowed into the enclaves, apart from food and medication, which are approved by the Main Staff." And if we go to the next page in B/C/S and stay where we are in English, do you see, right after -- sorry, we lost part of the B/C/S. If we could scroll to the left a little bit. Right under sub-part C, it says: "All authorised cargo and people (authorisation from the VRS Main Staff) is to be thoroughly checked at the following check-points." Do you see that, sir? It's about a third of the way down the page under sub-part C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's on top of the page, Mr. Thayer, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that. I see here that that is on the top of the page, that particular statement. "Detailed checks should be carried out at the following check-points of all authorised cargo and persons."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in English, but stay where we are in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Focusing on number 7, do you see number 7, sir: "All UNPROFOR movements to and from the enclaves without the authorisation of the VRS Main Staff are prohibited ..." Do you see that at number 7?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go to the next page in English. And we'll need to go to, I think, the next page in B/C/S for paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Focusing for a moment on paragraph 9, sir, we can see that General Zivanovic orders complete mining along the lines reached. He orders that a stone wall is to be built, or a wooden fence, so that the enclave would be completely surrounded, that is, fenced in, and so it would be made impossible for the Muslims to leave the enclave. And there's a reference to: "All artillery weapons, mortars of all calibres, and other means of fire backup are to be fortified at basic and reserve firing positions." Do you see those sections in paragraph 9, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 10, he orders that: "The brigade commands shall pay special attention to the training of snipers and to securing mufflers for sniper rifles so that each sniper rifle would have a muffler." Have you had a chance to --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the next page in English, and we can stay where we are in the B/C/S. And if we could blow up maybe paragraph 13, although we may lose part of it. So if we can't -- we can't do it in the B/C/S, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Focusing on paragraph 13, sir, we see that General Zivanovic states that: "Since the Muslim forces and UNPROFOR from the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa did not fulfill the discussed agreement on the demilitarisation of Muslim forces, and since they continue to move around armed and to open fire from infantry weapons and mortars against VRS soldiers and our population, the brigade command (independent infantry battalion) and units must take all measures to prevent that and to reduce the enclaves to the area listed in the agreement - Srebrenica (town), Zepa and Gorazde (the town and a three-kilometre area)." Let me know when you've had a chance to review that paragraph 13, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, based on your experience following Colonel Ognjenovic's report dated the 4th of July, and following the issuance of this order, can you tell us what -- first of all, what is this order about? We've just obviously read a number of portions. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the purpose of this order was, as you experienced the actions and activities of the Bratunac Brigade during this time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the content of the entire order, I wouldn't want to speak about it because, quite simply, I'd need a bit of time to read it all in detail and to analyse it. However, as for the particular points that we discuss now, that you have drawn my attention to, it has to do with spelling out, in specific terms, certain activities by way of orders of the Drina Corps that were sent to the Bratunac Brigade. Inter alia, as far as I can remember, the first point relates to the restriction of movement and the entry of convoys in the Srebrenica enclave. The second point, if I remember correctly, has to do with supplying -- or, rather, preventing movement and the communication between Muslims along these roads, Srebrenica-Zepa, Srebrenica-Kladanj, Srebrenica-Tuzla, and I think there's another road as well. And then the next point refers to the training and equipping of snipers in the mentioned units; inter alia, the Bratunac Brigade. That would be it, roughly, these basic points that you have drawn my attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience during this period of time, what was the purpose of these various measures that the Bratunac Brigade was ordered to take?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ultimate aim was to prevent, first of all, what was evident, when we're talking about convoys and restrictions relating to the entry of convoys. Since I know, even without this order, what it was about and what the subject of the restrictions was, in my opinion, the basic intent was, militarily speaking, to reduce the combat readiness of DutchBat to a minimum, in the sense that, in my view, and I'm speaking only from that aspect, what I think, and that is that so that the DutchBat would not be able to carry out the duties because of which it was there. The next thing is to create pressure on the Srebrenica enclave so that, simply, as many people as possible would leave the enclave. And the third thing was simply a complete blockade of the enclave, physical sealing off of the enclave, in order to create a chaotic situation in which life was impossible, simply unfit for people. That is my conclusion of sorts on the basics of what I could see from this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the one hand, we saw, in the order, the order to build walls, stone walls or wooden walls, to seal the enclave so that nobody could get out. And, on the other hand, you're saying one of the goals was to create conditions so that people would leave. Isn't that a contradiction? And if it is, if you can explain that. And if it's not, can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a contradiction, linguistically speaking. But the goal was for the enclave to disappear. That was the ultimate goal. Since I know General Zivanovic very well, when General Zivanovic writes that there should be fortifications around the enclave, that it should be hermetically sealed, I mean, I know his style, I know how General Zivanovic expressed himself. And the way it is stated in the order, and based on what I know, and I know the territory very well, practically with the forces that were there at the time, it was practically impossible to hermetically seal off the enclave, to prevent all communication, and anybody from getting out, and so on and so forth. So the sealing also meant that nobody could leave in an organised way, in units. As for individuals, there were certain routes - everyone knew that - which were used by people to move from the enclave towards Kladanj and from the enclave towards Tuzla. These are the directions leading through combat positions of my brigade, more or less, and that's what it states here, absolutely. It states that this should be closed off, but this was actually not possible to do. The declared goal and what you asked me about it being contradictory, yes, if I'm talking about it like that. But many people, Muslims, civilians, especially civilians from Srebrenica, wanted to leave Srebrenica. Many did leave. Many risked their lives and passed through minefields in order to leave that area and go to the free territory of Tuzla. So this was the case with many civilians. There is a difference between what is written here and what the actual situation was in the field. And just one sentence. I don't want to rule anything out. Perhaps General Zivanovic really did, and I don't want to get into that, and perhaps he did think that the territory should be closed off completely. Maybe he did think that. I don't want to go into that, because I don't know what General Zivanovic -- that, what he wrote, according to me, is practically impossible to achieve. And many people -- based on what I know, many civilians went to Zepa, went to Tuzla and went to Kladanj. I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 1908.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1908 shall be assigned Exhibit P2159 [Realtime transcript read in error "2155"]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've spoken a couple of times, sir, about sniping, so let's take a look at a --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just to correct the transcript, it should be Exhibit P2159. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 590 [sic], please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you sure that the number was recorded correctly, 590?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 5906, please. Sorry about that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, just have a look at this document. When you're ready to look at the next page, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go to the next page in B/C/S and the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While the Trial Chamber has a chance to just look at this second page, let me put a couple of preliminary questions to you, sir. We can see that this document, on its first page, was dated 10 July 1994. If we could go to the next page in English. We can see that it's signed by Marko Slijepcevic. Can you tell us who Mr. Slijepcevic was, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do recall. Marko Slijepcevic was the Technical Service desk officer in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the first page again in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see that the title of the document is "Status of sniper rifle, silencers, reconnaissance radars and infrared binoculars." Can you just tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what it states, the status of the rifles and all the other things that are mentioned with members of the Bratunac Brigade, the soldiers and the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we scroll down in the English a little bit, we can see that it lists the distribution of the sniper rifles by battalion. For example, we can see that there are four distributed to the 1st Battalion, and it looks like eight - and if we go to the second page in English - to the 2nd Battalion, and then a couple to the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of from which battalions the sniper activity that you've talked about originated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke several times in my previous testimony about the sniper activity. I told you that the positions of all the three infantry battalions were places from which sniper fire was opened, and agreements and terms of cease-fires and non-action in relation to the enclave were violated. So my answer is there was sniper fire from the positions of my brigade, from all positions of the area of responsibility of the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience, was there any battalion in particular from which the sniper fire originated more frequently than others?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In previous testimony, I talked about problems that I had with the 2nd Infantry Battalion. I don't want to rule out the possibility, or, rather, the specific situation. They were the closest to me, and I constantly had my eye on them. And they were directly in contact with Potocari, with the inhabited area, with the UNPROFOR base, the UNPROFOR check-point. They were within my range of sight. I was often in their positions, in their area of responsibility. I was familiar with all the details. And members of DutchBat most frequently complained, and we most frequently were resolving problems that arose because there was firing from the positions of the 2nd Battalion and they fired in front of their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were people killed by the sniping by the various Bratunac Brigade snipers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't give you specific examples. I don't recall any. It's been a long time since then. Each time when there were any casualties, when people were killed or wounded, I would speak with the members of DutchBat or with military observers. That was the opportunity to meet with them. We would not meet if there was fire without any consequences. That means that we met when fire was opened from the positions of my brigade, when there were any people injured, people killed, or people wounded, and we would also meet if the Muslims approached, and they did, and fired sniper fire at positions of the Bratunac Brigade, and also in cases when they would pass through certain areas outside of the enclave and fire at the population. So that means when there were killed, when there were wounded, we would meet, we would talk, we would investigate what happened, who did it, why they did it, and so on and so forth. And then, of course, we would report. This is something that I have to say. Each time, I had the obligation at each meeting -- actually, to report back about each meeting that was held and the reason why it was held to my superior command, in order to report to them or to ask for further instructions or orders in order to deal with the situation. This was something that I did regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who were the targets of this Bratunac Brigade sniping, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood the question correctly, who were the targets in the Bratunac Brigade, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No. Who were the targets of the Bratunac Brigade sniping? Who were the Bratunac Brigade snipers shooting at?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, I understand. If we're talking about overall activities, then there were different targets. It's true that Srebrenica was not a demilitarised zone and that there were members of the 28th Division of the Muslim forces at positions in Srebrenica and other positions. They opened fire a lot of the time, and fire was opened at those positions, those soldiers, soldiers who were on patrol, and there was also sniper action against them. As far as I was concerned, and also the UNPROFOR members, that was never a problem, because it was that kind of sniper fire that was part of the conflict. What was a problem was sniper fire at people, at civilians, at workers who were working, who were cultivating the land, doing their agricultural jobs, digging, doing things around their homesteads, and were not at positions, they were not armed. It's possible -- and I'm not ruling it out, but it is possible that somebody who was wounded in front of their house was a soldier, but at the point in time when they were doing something in front of their house, when they were making a facade or doing some construction work, they were not a soldier. We discussed that, and we had the problem why sniper fire was being directed at people who were not armed, who were not on the lines, who were in their yard, in their house, or they were working on their field, why was -- why were they targets of fire. This is something that we talked about. I'm sorry. There was such a case in the 3rd Infantry Battalion, and I do have information about that, because Mr. Vukota Vukovic -- we frequently privately, informally, generally sat down and talked. Thus, there was such situations in the 3rd Infantry Battalion. There were fewer such cases in the 1st Battalion, but the sniper fire and action against those who should not have been a target in any case was more pronounced in the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 5906.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we first go, please, to the last page of this document in both languages. We can see here a name, "Momir Nikolic." Is it your name, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What does it mean, that you are listed in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should -- or, actually, it means that I had a sniper -- I was issued a sniper and that I had it in my strong box in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it is true that you had one piece of this weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like it states there, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5906 shall be assigned Exhibit P2160. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go back one page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please stay with this document as it is. Judge Mindua would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There it is. Thank you. Witness, you confirmed that you were given a sniper rifle, a weapon. We know that snipers play a very important part in an army, and it's a well-recognised position. I would like to know whether you had been specially trained to use this weapon, and what were you, very specifically, assigned to do when you were given this weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure that I entirely understood you, but I will try to answer. I didn't complete any sniper training. I didn't fire the sniper anywhere. I didn't use it, the sniper rifle. But I am on the list. I can explain that. There were several officers, even some from logistics, who were issued the sniper rifle. Simply, the snipers came to the brigade. There were plenty of them in the depot as well outside of this list, so that I, as a security officer, was issued one. I had it in my office all the time like that. I never fired from that sniper rifle or did anything else. I never used it at any point in the manner that it is meant to be used, so the answer is I never went through training -- I am an infantryman, my specialty, but -- I am an officer, but I never went through any particular training, nor did I use it, and I did have it. And I was never the only one who had the sniper. I want to be quite honest. I had the privilege of being the chief of security, and I could ask the logistics guys to have such a rifle. And I did ask for one, and I got one, and I had it throughout that whole period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. Just now, in answer to Judge Mindua's question, you've stated that: "I never used it at any point in the manner that it is meant to be used ..." How is it meant to be used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I answered that question, and I will answer it again. A sniper rifle, as a weapon, is used -- a complete sniper with a sight is used to hit specific targets; mainly moving targets, live targets. That is the main characteristic of a sniper. I did take part in combat. I had an automatic rifle, 7.62 millimetres, that I used in combat. And like any officer, I carried the rifle with me all the time. I never was without it. When I went on assignment or on positions, I never went out unarmed. But, as I say, I never used the sniper rifle. I never took it into combat with me when I went. And I've said already that as far as I know, sniper rifles are used to fire at concrete, specific live targets, and "sniping" is the colloquial term for that particular type of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Does it mean, then, that you never used it because you never had the opportunity to use it, the occasion did not arise for you to use it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there were situations. In wartime, you can always find a situation in which you can use a sniper rifle. That means I could have behaved just like irresponsible soldiers for whom I requested sanctions and detention for sniping at targets that were not meant to be the targets of sniper fire. Snipers were used to fire at targets at positions and during combat. That would be a legal, legitimate target of those who were firing from sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you are going to move to another document, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Actually, I wasn't, Mr. President. I was just about to ask to move back one page. I see we're at the break. If I can just put this one question, then we can put this document away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can go back one page just in the English, and I just want to make sure that the record is as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've told us, obviously, about having been issued a sniper rifle. There's no dispute about that. I just want to make sure that the record is clear about what this document represents. If we look at Roman numeral V, and we just need to scroll down a little bit, do you see Roman numeral V, sir, where it refers to infrared binoculars being issued?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So we have, under Roman numeral V, there are two people who, according to this list, were issued infrared binoculars. Your name is listed at number 2. If we go to the next page in English. We can see that according to this document, you were issued with one set of infrared binoculars. Do you recall actually having a set of infrared or night-time binoculars, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, your name isn't on this list as being in possession of a sniper rifle. Do you recall approximately when you requested and were issued your sniper rifle, just so we have a clear record? Again, this is dated 10 July 1994. Do you remember approximately when you requested and you were issued your sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that my name is there in the document in relation to the sniper, but I want to talk about the actual state of affairs. I said before I did have a sniper in my office. It was in my strong box. And sometime in 1993, it was when I got it. These are infrared binoculars. I got that as a present from people who would come to the Bratunac Brigade. I also had that. Well, believe me, I didn't even know how to use it or anything like that. It was simply a set that was given to me by those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I see we're beyond the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. We must have our first break now, and we will resume five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have 65 ter 5991, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, take a moment to familiarise yourself with the document. Let us know when you're ready, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it. I didn't read it in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. What we have here is an intelligence report written by the assistant commander for intelligence, Captain Salihovic, of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the date is 3 July 1995. And I just want to focus on the top portion of that first paragraph, where he reports that: "Particularly, fierce sniper fire is coming from the direction of the Buljim ..." And he provides a trig point: "... Zeleni Jadar and Zalazje area, where one woman was killed by a sniper bullet yesterday." My question to you, sir, is: Are you familiar with these three areas, Buljim, this trig point that's listed, Zeleni Jadar and Zalazje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about those facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are these areas all within the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber which battalion or battalions would have been responsible for these particular areas?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I don't have a map at hand, but the Zeleni Jadar facility was covered by the 3rd Infantry Battalion, and I think that to a smaller extent, it was also covered by the Independent Battalion from Skelani. Zalazje, as far as I know, was within the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, while Buljim -- Ravni Buljin was, in the beginning, covered by the 1st Infantry Battalion. And in this period, approximately, elevation 820 at Ravni Buljin, there was also an attached and re-subordinated battalion from the Zvornik Brigade, but this battalion was then within the Bratunac Brigade. I explained it yesterday. It means that it was within the Bratunac Brigade, as far as command and control goes, and also as far as the logistical support was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 5991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 5991 shall be assigned Exhibit P2161. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn to another topic now, and that was the involvement of yourself, as chief of intelligence and security affairs of the Bratunac Brigade, with respect to the movement of humanitarian aid and DutchBat resupply convoys into and out of the Srebrenica enclave. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber how the convoy process worked, as you experienced it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to attempt to explain, very briefly, what I know about what was going on in the zone of responsibility of my unit, my brigade. When we talk about Srebrenica as a protected area, I can say that various convoys often arrived at Srebrenica, and I would like to describe them now. There were convoys related to the needs of the Dutch Battalion. They were their convoys, which brought in food and other materiel, equipment, fuel, and everything else that was necessary for their proper functioning. Then there were convoys entering the Srebrenica zone organised by the UNHCR. They were humanitarian convoys, and the load was intended for the civilian population of Srebrenica. Then there was something that it wasn't really convoys. They were trucks and jeeps supplying the international military observers, then Medecins Sans Frontieres and other international organisations that were present in Srebrenica. All those convoys would enter with the approval of the superior command. In this case, it was I who received documents in the brigade command with the signature of the co-ordinating body or the signature of General Milovanovic, who was the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff. These documents, these approvals or notifications, contained a very precise description of what was supposed to enter the Srebrenica enclave within a convoy; for example, the number of trucks, their registration numbers, specification of cargo, amount. Everything was specified in those permits. The convoys that would originate in Croatia - I remember that there was a number of convoys coming from Zagreb - would usually be controlled at the point where they enter the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was usually in Karakaj. As far as I know, a detailed control of those convoys would be performed in Karakaj. And now a few words about the Yellow Bridge, Zuti Most. I have to explain what the Yellow Bridge is. That's a place between Bratunac and Potocari. If it is necessary, if Your Honours deem that that is necessary, I can draw a diagram to show you how it looked like. It was a check-point manned by the military police and some people whose sole task was the control of the convoys. That check-point was the place where a control would be performed in accordance with the evaluation of the convoy. They didn't always do a detailed control of the convoy there at the Yellow Bridge because the detailed control would have always been done at the point of entry to Bosnia-Herzegovina. We always controlled the convoys there. At the Yellow Bridge, we would perform a detailed control of all the convoys leaving Srebrenica, going towards Zagreb or other places. As for the obligations of my brigade, all the duties and obligations of my brigade were defined in the orders issued by the Drina Corps Command. I would even say that sometimes we would receive direct orders from the Main Staff. But in most cases, all the instructions and all our obligations would be defined in the orders coming from the Drina Corps Command. As for my personal involvement in this, within my competency and within the tasks assigned to me by my commander, I would be engaged on some of the controls. I wasn't always present at those controls, but I was present quite often; when it was necessary or when I deemed that my presence was necessary. Also, in the period leading up to the operation, itself, I received several orders and instructions specifying that a detailed check and the control should be performed, and in those cases I had the duty to be present. At that check-point, there was a permanent team from the Bratunac Brigade and one or two policemen who would change their posts depending on their shifts. So this was my short description of the entry of the convoys, the controls that we performed, and the orders on the basis of which we carried out our tasks related to the convoys that would enter or leave the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we saw earlier this morning the order from July 1994 from General Zivanovic, which, among other things, spoke about regulating the convoys coming in, restricting the movement of UNPROFOR members, and so forth. And you testified that the measures that were being ordered in that order from General Zivanovic were intended to have the effect of increasing the pressure on the enclave. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber whether or how the convoy procedure that you were a part of contributed in any way to that pressure on the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to be precise. That previous order that I looked at, if we are now talking about the same issue, contains an item saying that the entry of everything into the enclave would be limited, except items related to food. I'm now paraphrasing. I don't remember the exact language. And it also says that entries into the enclave should be in accordance with the order of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. That is, briefly, the essence of that item. And, indeed, my role, the role of a person who was at the check-point, working and performing checks together with the police and the personnel from my brigade, was nothing else but carrying out the order that was received, while observing all the conditions defined in that order. For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I want to emphasise one thing. We observed every order that would arrive in written form. There were no problems, because such written orders would contain everything that we had to do, and we only had to observe it and carry it out. However, in the days leading up to the operations, as I had -- as I said a little bit earlier, there were cases that some orders were transmitted through the telephone and that some of the notifications that we had received in written form would then be amended or changed. In the beginning, I would solve such situations, when they became more frequent, by obtaining the approval of the commander of my brigade. The person who worked at the check-point, who was the duty officer at the check-point, Jovan Ivic [phoen] - he used to teach the Russian language - would normally get in touch directly with the Drina Corps Command. I don't know exactly who was in charge there in the command -- in that command for the humanitarian end, but he would call that person directly from the Yellow Bridge, and then he would solve any problem that would arise because of the fact that some of the orders arrived verbally through the telephone and not as a written document, and that contributed to the normal passage -- that contributed to making the situation worse, when it relates to the normal passage of the convoys. Now, you're asking me how that contributed to the situation in the enclave. I can tell you that the effect was negative. I can tell you that it had negative influence to all the representatives of the international organisations present in Srebrenica, because for them, that was the only way to resupply. They had no other way to resupply them. And the representatives of the UNHCR would especially highlight the problem related to the entry of the convoys, which were intended for the population, and which were then detained at the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I'm going to try to save a little bit of time. I have some documents to show you. I'm going to try to move through them quickly. The first thing I want to do, to try to save some time as well, is just to put up on the screen some of your prior testimony, and I'll just read it into the record, since it's not translated, and see what you have to say about it on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 7301 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I would like to draw your attention on your witness summary you provided the Chamber with. This is especially focused on the events in July 1995, just to remind you about the time we've already used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go to page 32966, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, just to clarify, this is a document under seal. If you will use parts of this document which are under seal, you should indicate that it should not be broadcast and not read out in the court in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I will. We were in open session for this portion, so I think we're safe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to read your answer to a question that was put to you in the Popovic trial and ask you if you have anything to add to it or take away from it. You said there, and this is at page 32966, starting at line 9: "There were such acts that contributed to the fact that these international organisations and Dutch Battalion became or were rendered incapacitated for carrying out their mandate in the enclave. First of all, I have in mind the absolute and total blockade of -- put on supply lines, first of all to the Dutch Battalion, starting from food, weapons, equipment, ammunition, and everything else that in total contributes to full combat readiness of a unit and its capacity to do its job that it's deployed to do. This blockade was effected by stopping the entry into Srebrenica by convoys, the prevention of rotation of units and companies that were replaced periodically, preventing the supply of fuel for APCs and other vehicles that the Dutch troops had." Do you remember giving that answer in the Popovic trial, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember that. However, either I received a bad interpretation of your question or I misunderstood you. In your previous question, I understood you to ask me whether these limitations had a negative effect on the enclave, and I said that all these limitations on the convoys, and obstructions, and misunderstandings does have a negative effect, and that's true. Now, if you ask me what exactly were the effects of that ban, what exactly was banned, and what exactly we did, then I'm going to tell you what you just read out to me. In this period of time just before the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, every day the measures would be more and more restrictive. I already explained that written permissions to enter the enclave would often arrive as written documents, and then there would be additional instructions coming as verbal instructions, telling us to hinder or to prevent the entry. So I would like to repeat this once again. I am the person who knew what was going into Srebrenica and in what quantities. I had my estimates, which were pretty accurate, estimates of the number of people there, both civilians and soldiers. When we talk about the representatives of international organisations, since I was checking them entering and leaving the enclave, I knew exactly what were the numbers of those international representatives in the enclave. So if, within a certain time-period, you have a limit for the fuel for APCs, and then, according to my estimates, not even 10 per cent would enter the enclave, and I'm talking about the 10 per cent of the quantity that I, as a layman, would consider the necessary quantity, if everything that they want to obtain, such as ammunition and other things, is limited, and if they tell me every time, when they get in touch with me, what they need, and they request me, they ask me to try to organise that their request would be granted, and if I know all this, I can then very easily arrive at the conclusion -- I, as a soldier, can very easily conclude that all these restrictions were introduced with a view to decrease the combat readiness of the Dutch Battalion within the enclave. And then, of course, if the Dutch Battalion does not have enough fuel for their armoured carriers, they cannot perform their patrols, they cannot move around as much as they would need to, and in that period there was a number of problems in the enclave that they had to control and there was a number of skirmishes within the enclave. I knew about it, they told me about it. And if you are then reduced to the situation that you have to ask the Serbian side things that you don't have, then obviously you are not in the situation to do everything that you have to do. So I already said it, and I still stand behind what I said. All these problems influenced the combat readiness of the Dutch Battalion. They also influenced the overall situation within the enclave. And I want to mention just one more thing. If there is a company, and you don't allow for this company to leave the enclave and rotate the personnel, then you can imagine what was the situation like inside the enclave, how dissatisfied those people waiting for the replacement were, and they wouldn't get such a permission. I spoke about all that in my previous testimony, and I still stand by all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you -- when you say that the restrictions also influenced the overall situation within the enclave, what are you referring to when you refer to the overall situation in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I've already responded to that question, but let me say this once again. I have mentioned different types of convoys. If a convoy with civilians does not -- or, rather, a supply convoy for civilians does not enter, you can imagine what kind of chaos that will cause in the enclave, if they did not get enough flour, oil, or whatever else they were supposed to receive by way of aid. If the Dutch Battalion does not get enough fuel, then it is certain that the commander of the Dutch Battalion cannot carry out the tasks that he had planned. If the units involved cannot be replaced on time, then you're going to have dissatisfaction among the members of that unit. So all of this has an adverse effect on the situation in the enclave, and the situation in the enclave, to the best of my knowledge, was very difficult as it was. In the Srebrenica territory, according to my assessments, in Srebrenica there was always between 35 and 40, and, in a certain period of time, 60.000 persons all together in that area that was rather limited. Of course, not to speak about the other aspect now, and that is supplies, it was very hard to live and work there and carry out combat tasks in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your testimony on the situation in the enclave relates to what period, given that in one of your statements, you are quoted as saying that the armed conflict alleged in the indictment referred to the armed conflict that began on the 6th of April, 1992, and ended with the Dayton Peace Agreement signed on 14 December? So, specifically, this situation you are describing is for which period? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation in Srebrenica, since my primary task as that of an intelligence officer was to follow the overall situation in the enclave in Srebrenica, including monitoring the activities of the military forces or, rather, the forces of the 28th Division, then I was aware of the situation roughly. So these are intelligence estimates. I was aware of the situation. I spoke to you about the difficult situation in the enclave of Srebrenica. Well, what I can say to you is that I can speak in more specific terms about the period just before the attack against the Srebrenica enclave. However, to the best of my knowledge, the situation in Srebrenica was no different from when Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised zone all the way up to the fall of the enclave; that is to say, this entire period from sometime in April 1993 all the way up until the fall of the enclave. In Srebrenica, to the best of my knowledge, it was very difficult. It was very difficult to live there. People -- Srebrenica, there was no electricity, there was no water, there was no food. They only had what they could manufacture themselves and what they would receive from the UNHCR. That period from the moment when the enclave was declared as such, up until the fall of the enclaves, at some point it would get a bit better or a bit worse, but, on the whole, the situation was very difficult in the enclave, from the point of view of health, and food, and footwear, equipment, anything. That is what I knew about the enclave of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I've understood you well, there was a control, a check-up, and restrictive measures for the convoy of the DutchBat, and through these activities, your brigade and the VRS were able to control the activities of the DutchBat, and they could also control the life of people in the Srebrenica enclave. This is what you have said. And you were in charge of the security of this brigade, and you were in charge of this policy. Is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If your question was whether I inherited, as it were, such orders, then the answer is yes. In the testimony I have provided to date, I have said a countless number of times that I followed these orders, and the control that you are speaking of is one that had been ordered from the Command of the Drina Corps or, rather, the Main Staff. I, as the person carrying out the order in the field, acted exactly in accordance with the order as defined. Personally, or privately, as it were, I was not opposed to that. I didn't make things any more difficult or any easier, in view of the overall situation. I behaved in accordance with the orders of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Well, in fact, you preempted my next question. I wanted to know whether this was a deliberate policy from the VRS and from your brigade. I'm thinking about the restrictions for the DutchBat, and I think that you will answer with a yes to this question. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the answer is going to be yes, because absolutely -- I mean, well, I wouldn't want to speak about politics now. I, as a soldier, believe that that is no policy. These are specific military measures aimed at attaining the desired objective; namely, that conditions to be created in the enclave are those desired. If you believe that that is a policy, then that was a policy of my brigade and of the army, or, rather, the superior commands that took part in this through writing orders. I participated in that through the execution of orders issued by my superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, you see that I am constantly taking notes. And in my notes, this is what I've written: You complained several times to the DutchBat regarding groups of Muslim fighters who were leaving the enclave in order to attack Serb targets outside the enclave. Yesterday, you told us that you put forward several complaints to the DutchBat about this. At the same time, today you're now telling us that you had to prevent the DutchBat from functioning in a normal way through the restrictions to the convoys. And I would, therefore, like to put a question to you. Why did you complain to the DutchBat then? Was this a farce? Were you acting in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this was interpreted properly to me, I think that these two questions of yours addressed to me cannot be brought into the same context, as far as I'm concerned. And the fact that I complained to the Dutch has nothing to do with it, the fact that I indicated to them that they were leaving the enclave and firing at various positions. And Srebrenica was a demilitarised zone, at that. I mean, to this day I claim that every time when the Muslim forces left the zone and killed people on the separation line, and opened sniper fire at civilians, I was quite right in asking to have that stopped and prevented. As for these activities of the Muslim armed forces, I, as a soldier, don't see that as related at all to this other question that you have put to me; before the operation of Srebrenica, that I carried out the order of my superior command; that the entry of fuel, ammunition, et cetera, be restricted, I really cannot relate the two at all. In the latter case, I simply carried out the orders that I had received, and in the first case, I protected my very own unit from the activity of armed Muslims, Muslims who were supposed to have been disarmed, but were not, in actual fact. The Dutch Battalion was against that, and they kept starting actions to take away weapons and stopping the members of the 28th Muslim unit to fire at us. That was the situation on the ground as it was. That's what I did throughout, from the moment when I was appointed liaison officer all the way up until the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. But a few members of the DutchBat came here, and they said that they didn't have sufficient means. And if I establish the link between the two, I can understand that when they said they didn't have any means, they didn't have sufficient fuel, or food, or equipment, and this was the result of the restrictions that you imposed. There is a link between the two, I think. This is, in fact, my opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree with you. I can only agree with one part of your statement; namely, that that can be linked up in the period just before the operation. However, I disagree with you in terms of this being related to the entire period that started when the status of enclave was granted. It wasn't the members of DutchBat or UNPROFOR who were without fuel throughout their tour there, and it wasn't that restrictions were imposed against them. During most of their tour in Srebrenica, they were regularly supplied with ammunition, fuel, food, et cetera, and rotations took place regularly. So over a long period of time of their stay there, there can be no mention of any restrictions. In that period when there were no restrictions, the Dutch soldiers were not in a position to control the Muslim armed forces that were in the enclave.
